title: Welcome to the N.H.K.
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Tatsuhiro Sato, a 22-year-old university dropout, has been a hikikomori (shut-in) for years and blames a conspiracy he calls the N.H.K. A mysterious girl, Misaki, offers to 'cure' him through nightly counseling sessions, while his otaku neighbor Yamazaki drags him into writing an erotic video game. Drugs, a pyramid scheme, an online suicide pact and his own paranoia pull him down before a fragile bond with Misaki gives both a reason to go on.
life_message: It holds up the halting, unheroic step of staying alive and reaching out to one other person.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Shame drives Sato inward, but no one seeks retaliation; disputes are internal.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Sato lives outside work or school structures, free and adrift.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rescue comes from friends and a stranger more than family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Senpai Hitomi and the others are peers in failure; little rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Psychology lectures and conspiracy-busting, little religion.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Pressure to work and survive meets otaku self-expression.

folkways.japan: Hikikomori, NEET status and social pressure to conform to work and school paths are specifically Japanese social phenomena the story examines.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Santos: sharp satirical tone mixing bleak drama and comedy, skewering online gaming and multi-level marketing.
delivery.note: Its critique of escapism and exploitation is carried by satire of what traps Sato, per the review.

winners_losers: No one wins outright; Sato and Misaki survive by leaning on each other. Sympathy goes to the isolated, while escapist otaku culture, drugs and pyramid schemes are shown as traps.
